audits.question: Check the entry's Etruscan language/alphabet relationship using epigraphic or scholarly evidence; readable adapted Greek letters do not establish Indo-European affiliation or complete lexical understanding.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/etruria.md §2, lines 41-51: table rows Genealogy, Script ancestry, Sign selection (lines 41-43); bullet "Not 'an undeciphered alphabet'" (line 49); bullet "Shared alphabet, shared loanword, similar deity, and shared ancestry are four different relationships" (line 51)
audits.entry_claim: Entry asserts: Etruscan is non-Indo-European, with its relationship to Raetic and Lemnian under Tyrsenian/Tyrrhenian well supported while exact branching, separation dates, and migration scenarios are less secure ([R98]; [B02]); its alphabet was adapted from the Euboean Greek tradition with sign selection reshaped to Etruscan phonology (a/e/i/u without Greek o; Greek voiced-stop letters not retained as a b/d/g series), so script descent is not language descent ([M22]); letters and numerous formulas are readable while much vocabulary and connected-text interpretation remain uncertain, readability, grammatical analysis, and fluent translation being different achievements ([B02]; [T08]); a Greek-looking name or a shared alphabet does not make Etruscan Indo-European.
audits.source_citation: Posth, C., Zaro, V., Spyrou, M. A., et al. (2021), "The origin and legacy of the Etruscans through a 2000-year archeogenomic time transect", Science Advances 7(39): eabi7673, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abi7673, open-access copy at PubMed Central PMC8462907
audits.source_locator: Abstract and Introduction: "its extinct language, a non-Indo-European language not yet fully understood"; "the persistence of a probable non-Indo-European language isolate surrounded by Italic Indo-European-speaking groups (such as the Latins) is an intriguing and still unexplained phenomenon"; Abstract: "the putative non-Indo-European-speaking Etruscans"
audits.source_excerpt: its extinct language, a non-Indo-European language not yet fully understood ... the persistence of a probable non-Indo-European language isolate surrounded by Italic Indo-European-speaking groups (such as the Latins)
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the PubMed Central open-access copy after the host WebSearch lane returned HTTP 403 (quota); full page text retrieved and searched for language-affiliation wording; excerpts quoted from retrieved page text, not from search snippets
audits.basis: Component mapping of the bounded entry claim to retrieved evidence: (1) non-Indo-European affiliation — primary source's own wording quoted above, peer-reviewed (Science Advances 2021, PMC open-access copy). (2) incomplete lexical understanding despite readable letters — same passage "not yet fully understood", corroborated by BMCR 2008.05.37 (retrieved): "the Etruscan language is generally knowable" yet "multiple variant translations exist for many terms", Liber Linteus with "about 1330 words, but only about 50 major terms (30-40% is lost)", and "we should not expect polished translations". (3) alphabet adapted from the Euboean Greek tradition with reshaped sign selection (no o; no retained b/d/g series), i.e. script descent decoupled from language descent — Mnamon SNS page (retrieved, the entry's own [M22]): "The Euboean-Chalcidian variant of the Greek alphabet ... was at first adopted in its entirety by the Etruscans"; "a selection of the signs ... excluded the voiced plosives (beta and delta) and the vowel /o/"; syncope examples "Menrva instead of Menerva" and "turce in the place of turuce". (4) Tyrsenian relationship well supported with branching/dates less secure — Tyrsenian survey (retrieved, tertiary; the entry's declared bibliography check for [R98]): Rix 1998 proposal "has gained acceptance in scholarship"; split dates disputed (Rix: last quarter 2nd millennium BC; de Simone/Marchesini: before the Bronze Age; a late van der Meer 2004 split "has garnered little consensus"); "Etruscan: 13,000 inscriptions". The negative test in the question holds: no retrieved source derives Indo-European affiliation from the readable adapted Greek letters, and the peer-reviewed source itself pairs non-IE status with explicit incomplete understanding.
audits.coupling_implication: The entry's §2 coupling levers stand as written: script ancestry and language genealogy are separate relationships, so a fictional culture can borrow an alphabet without genealogical language consequence; the evidence-class ladder (attested readable letters vs supported vs contested interpretation) matches the sources' own pairing of non-IE status with 'not yet fully understood'. No downstream change required in language/dress/cult couplings from this audit.
audits.limits: The primary passage is a genetics paper's characterizations of the language, not a linguistic argument; its loose 'language isolate' phrasing is not a position on the Rix Tyrsenian grouping, which is instead corroborated only at tertiary level (Wikipedia Tyrsenian survey, which the entry itself used solely as a bibliography check for [R98]). Print works [B02], [R98], [ET91] were not consulted (no full-text access); [M22] and [T08] corroboration pages are the entry's own already-cited web sources, freshly re-fetched. The alphabet-adaptation component rests on Mnamon's synthesis, not on a newly inspected inscription photograph. A De Gruyter fetch of Freeman 1999 (Etruscan Studies) failed (JavaScript wall) and was abandoned without grinding; no restricted-work content was redistributed. All readings are author-side, not independent promotion verification.

audits.question: Check the Liber Linteus textile-text object biography and ritual-calendar interpretation against a museum/research source; distinguish original writing/use, later Egyptian mummy reuse, date and garment inference.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/etruria.md §8, lines 140-146: object-biography bullet (140); dating bullet (141); layout-and-interpretation bullet (142); LL 8.3 disagreement bullet (144); mummy-identity bullet (145); non-identification bullet (146)
audits.entry_claim: Entry asserts: the longest surviving Etruscan text is written on linen cut into strips and reused as wrapping for a female mummy acquired in Egypt in the nineteenth century, with mummy and linen now associated with the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb ([LL07]; [T08]); van der Meer proposes writing around 200-150 BCE from letter forms and a north-Etruscan context, with textile dating and the later mummy's dating as separate questions and no exact place or year claimed; the surviving layout is twelve inscribed columns, damaged and incomplete, black writing with red divisions/rubrics, whose calendar dates, repeated formulas, divine recipients, and offerings support interpretation as a ritual calendar, not an Egyptian funerary composition; at LL 8.3 Bonfante's 'twenty-sixth' versus van der Meer's '24th' evidences translation uncertainty; the mummy is not established as Etruscan, priestess, author, or carrier, and the transfer route remains uncertain.
audits.source_citation: Jean MacIntosh Turfa (2008), review of L. Bouke van der Meer, Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis: The Linen Book of Zagreb. A Comment on the Longest Etruscan Text (Peeters, 2007), Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2008.05.37 (the entry's own [T08])
audits.source_locator: Review body, 'Liber linteus' section (mummy purchased in Egypt 1848-49, came to Zagreb 1862; C-14 query; van der Meer p. 23 quotation; 12 columns; black ink of burnt ivory with vermilion rubrics; bandage strips) and 'Discrepancies with other translators' (LL 8.3)
audits.source_excerpt: found re-used as the wrappings of a female mummy of Ptolemaic-Roman date ... 'almost certainly written in Perugia or in its region, between c. 200 and 150 BC'
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the public BMCR review (entry's cited [T08]); full review text retrieved and quoted from the page text; corroborated by a FetchURL of the Wikipedia Liber Linteus article; Archaeological Museum in Zagreb homepage also fetched but carries no object content (reachability only)
audits.basis: Component mapping of the bounded entry claim to retrieved evidence: (1) object biography — BMCR: "A female mummy purchased in Egypt in 1848-49 by an Austro-Hungarian diplomat came in 1862 to Zagreb"; "the linen book found re-used as the wrappings of a female mummy of Ptolemaic-Roman date, now lovingly restored and displayed in the Arheoloski Muzej in Zagreb"; "The single large textile had been cut into horizontal strips to form bandages for the mummy". (2) separated datings — BMCR: "Recent C-14 results suggest the textile may have been woven as early as the 4th c. BC, although ... there is reason to query this"; inscription "almost certainly written in Perugia or in its region, between c. 200 and 150 BC" (van der Meer p. 23, quoted); "The mummy is probably Late Ptolemaic/1st c. BC"; corroboration: Wikipedia Liber Linteus: paleographic "approximately 250 BC" and C-14 "390 BC +/- 45 years" for the textile. (3) layout and ritual-calendar reading, not an Egyptian funerary composition — BMCR: "12 parallel columns", "black ink (of burnt ivory) with rubrics and dividers of vermilion (cinnabar)", "columns 2 through 12 contain a serial listing of rituals, some dated by months of the year" (18 June in Column 6; 13 August before late September in Column 8); Wikipedia corroborates ("twelve columns from right to left", "Black ink ... main text, and red ink for lines and diacritics", dates 18 June 6.14 and September 24 8.2) and records Krall's 1892 first identification as Etruscan after an initial Book-of-the-Dead misreading. (4) LL 8.3 translation-uncertainty exemplar — BMCR quotes Bonfante "twenty-sixth" against van der Meer "on 24th September sacrificial victims for Nethuns ...", exactly the entry's line-144 disagreement. (5) mummy-identity and transfer-route limits — BMCR: "(see 5-9 for colorful theories on mechanisms by which an Etruscan book reached Egypt.)"; "We cannot be sure that the LL reflects all cults in a universal fashion"; Wikipedia: the Nesi-hensu papyrus "postdates the mummy by nearly a century, which could suggest that the mummy is not Nesi-hensu". (6) no seamless translation / no garment inference — BMCR: "about 1330 words, but only about 50 major terms (30-40% is lost)", "we should not expect polished translations"; on cloth choice the reviewer speculates and marks it as speculation ("Perhaps because it derives from the sphere of women, or simply because it could be used outdoors ..."), supporting the entry's refusal to convert the linen medium into a garment or uniform claim.
audits.coupling_implication: The entry's staged object biography (book, cut textile, mummy wrapping, museum text) and its ritual-calendar interpretation are externally corroborated by the entry's own cited peer-reviewed review, freshly re-fetched; the entry's design lever — one textile passing through sacred-information, portable-property, burial-material, and archaeological-puzzle stages while the deceased's identity stays indeterminate — is exactly what the sources support, and the linen medium licenses no garment-form or pan-Etruscan cult-book inference.
audits.limits: The primary source is a peer-reviewed book review (secondary scholarship in a peer-reviewed venue), not the Peeters monograph [LL07] itself, which was not consulted; the museum-object record proper (Archaeological Museum in Zagreb 'The Zagreb Mummy' page, archived 2016) was not retrieved this session — the AMZ homepage fetch confirms site reachability only and is not counted as object confirmation, so no museum-object kind is claimed. Locator-level nuance recorded rather than harmonized: Wikipedia cites van der Meer p. 4 for 'approximately 250 BC' paleographic dating, while BMCR quotes van der Meer p. 23 for 'between c. 200 and 150 BC'; the entry follows T08/LL07 p. 23. The entry's 'acquired in Egypt in the nineteenth century' matches BMCR's 1848-49 purchase. Raw source pages were read but not stored in the deliverable; all readings are author-side, not independent promotion verification.
